source: Weber, Binder, Krauss (2018) Why can only 24% solve Bayesian reasoning problems in natural frequencies
finding: The paper restates the McDowell and Jacobs (2017) meta-analysis: natural frequencies lift Bayesian accuracy from about 4% (probability format) to about 24%. Three of four people still fail even in the helpful format.
numbers: Meta-analytic means: 4% (probabilities) vs 24% (natural frequencies), per problem. Worked example: base rate 0.01%, sensitivity 100%, false alarm 0.19%, true answer 5% (10 of 200).
quote: on average three quarters of participants in their meta-analysis failed to obtain the correct solution for such a task in frequency format
limits: Secondary report of the meta-analysis; the original (Psychological Bulletin 143, 1273-1312) was not opened. Means hide large spread across studies and samples.
agent_relevance: Never expect a plain-probability Bayes step to be right by default. Force the agent to rebuild every conditional-probability problem as counts out of a fixed reference population before answering.

source: Weber, Binder, Krauss (2018) Why can only 24% solve Bayesian reasoning problems in natural frequencies
finding: Many people given natural frequencies translate them back into probabilities. What people calculate with predicts success better than how the task was shown.
numbers: N=180 (first sample 114 in 2016, replication sample 66 after exclusions, same effects in both). When the task was in natural frequencies, 49% still calculated with probabilities. When in probabilities, only 18% switched to frequencies. Overall frequencies were the calculation format in 34% of 360 tasks. Heroin problem correct: frequencies shown and used 61%; probabilities shown but frequencies used 53%; probabilities used 13% (shown as probabilities) and 9% (shown as frequencies).
limits: Mostly maths-education students (over 80%), so numeracy is high; 42 teacher-track students got 50% vs 21% for the rest. Paper-and-pencil, German school context. GLMM: presentation format b=-3.04, p=.13 (n.s.); calculation format b=9.85, p=.01; marginal R2 0.065, conditional R2 0.685, so person differences dominate.
agent_relevance: Format helps only if the agent actually computes in counts. A scaffold step should check the working format, not just the prompt format. Also a built-in replication inside one paper that held.

source: Weber, Binder, Krauss (2018) Why can only 24% solve Bayesian reasoning problems in natural frequencies
finding: Context changes difficulty. Same format, different story, very different accuracy.
numbers: Presented in natural frequencies: heroin problem 51% correct (n=87 inferences), car accident problem 22% (n=92). Probability format: 22% (n=92) vs 19% (n=89). Pooled 20% (probabilities) vs 36% (frequencies).
limits: Two problems only; the content and the numbers differ across them, so context and numbers are confounded.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a single worked example to show the agent is calibrated on Bayes. Test across several scenario types and number sizes.

source: Shengelia & Lagnado (2021) Are jurors intuitive statisticians? Bayesian causal reasoning in legal contexts
finding: In a rich legal case (parents accused of abusing a baby; a rare blood disorder is the alternative cause) people moved their beliefs the right way with each new piece of evidence, but not by the Bayesian amount. They ignored the supplied base rates and set their own, much higher priors.
numbers: Experiment 1: 155 MTurk participants. Evidence stage main effect on abuse judgments F(2.545,315.587)=85.30, p<.001, partial eta2=.408; on disorder judgments F(2.293,284.339)=479.27, partial eta2=.794. Subjective priors (abuse M=0.534, disorder M=0.267) were far above the stated base rates (0.01 and 0.001). Observed judgments differed significantly from each person's own Bayesian model at every evidence stage.
limits: Online US sample, one case vignette, sequential presentation. Bayesian norms were computed from each person's own priors and own causal model, which is lenient. Experiment 2 had N=93.
agent_relevance: Direction of update is robust; size is not. Let the agent use evidence in the right direction, but compute likelihood ratios and posterior odds explicitly instead of trusting felt strength.

source: Shengelia & Lagnado (2021) Are jurors intuitive statisticians? Bayesian causal reasoning in legal contexts
finding: Telling people the two causes may both be true or both false (non-exclusive, non-exhaustive) did not change updating. Errors partly follow zero-sum thinking: evidence for one cause is counted against the other.
numbers: Experiment 1: no main effect of condition for abuse, F(2,124)=1.20, p=.304, or disorder, F(2,124)=0.13, p=.881. Experiment 2 (N=93) added an explicit reminder before each judgment. Under-weighting after the bruising evidence and over-weighting after the positive blood test were both seen.
limits: The authors explain the errors with zero-sum reasoning (Pilditch et al. 2019); this is an interpretation, not a direct test. A reminder alone did not remove it.
agent_relevance: A generic instruction to consider other causes is weak. The scaffold needs an explicit step: list competing hypotheses and score each piece of evidence under each, including 'other cause'.

source: Shengelia & Lagnado (2021) Are jurors intuitive statisticians? Bayesian causal reasoning in legal contexts
finding: Background reviewed in the paper: base-rate neglect is reduced when the problem is shown as a causal structure (Krynski & Tenenbaum 2007), when base rates are frequencies or learned by experience (Koehler 1996). Quantitative updating is conservative in many studies, but Thompson et al. (2013) argue that earlier work overstated the conservatism through method problems.
numbers: Qualitative claims only; no new numbers. Conservatism: Phillips & Edwards 1966, Peterson & Beach 1967, Rottman & Hastie 2014 cited. Gap between observed and Bayesian updating grows with the amount of evidence (Schum 1966, cited).
limits: Claims about other papers are taken from this paper's literature review; the originals were not opened. The conservatism-versus-not debate is open.
agent_relevance: Give the agent a causal graph of the case (hypothesis, mechanisms, alternative causes) before it weighs evidence.

source: Sidebotham (2025) Flipping the conditional: why we are probably wrong about probabilities
finding: Plain statement of the prosecutor's fallacy as flipping the conditional: P(evidence | innocent) is mistaken for P(innocent | evidence). It is most tempting when the evidence probability is tiny. The same slip drives misreading of p-values and test sensitivity.
numbers: No empirical numbers. Examples: Sally Clark (two infant deaths), UK nurse Lucy Letby statistical evidence. Leopard example: P(four legs | leopard)=1, P(leopard | four legs) near 0.
limits: Narrative review in a paediatric anaesthesia journal, no new data. The Letby statistical evidence is still disputed, so use it as an example of the error type, not as settled fact.
agent_relevance: Useful test item set for the agent: a check that asks 'which way does this conditional run?' before any rare-event argument is accepted.

source: Feeny & Stamboulid (2026) Sally Clark: trial and error by judge and jury
finding: The 1 in 73 million figure was wrong for three separate reasons, only one being arithmetic: it squared a single-death rate (assumes independence), it used a residual diagnosis (SIDS) as if it explained one case, and it was never compared with the chance of the rival explanation (double murder).
numbers: Figure: about 1 in 73 million for two natural infant deaths. Hill (2004), cited: after one SIDS death the risk of a second is 6 to 10 times higher than in families with none. Royal Statistical Society (Oct 2001 news release, Jan 2002 letter) called the squaring 'statistically invalid'. Appeal quashed 2003.
limits: Legal-methods commentary; the Hill numbers are quoted from this paper, not opened. The paper argues the fault was in the whole admission process, not only the number.
agent_relevance: The decisive repair is comparative: always put the evidence probability under every live explanation. That is the likelihood-ratio step in the schema, not a one-sided rarity argument.

source: Feeny & Stamboulid (2026), citing Dawid on Sally Clark
finding: If background rates of double deaths from natural causes are relevant, background rates of double deaths from murder are equally relevant. Presenting only one is irrational and prejudicial (Dawid, as reported).
numbers: Qualitative. No new numbers beyond the 1 in 73 million figure.
limits: Second-hand report of Dawid's argument; Dawid's paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: Template for a guardrail: any 'this is very unlikely by chance' claim triggers a request for the rival-hypothesis probability.

source: Juror comprehension of forensic expert testimony: a literature review and gap analysis (2019)
finding: Across studies, laypeople under-weight statistical evidence rather than over-weight it. Both numeric and verbal likelihood ratios move belief in the right direction but far less than the expert intended.
numbers: Martire et al. as reported: belief change over 350,000 times smaller than the expert intended. Kaye & Koehler review: jurors tend to underweight statistical evidence. McQuiston-Surrett & Saks: belief rose after population-rate data, but less than expected.
limits: Review of other people's studies, secondary. 'Orders of magnitude' compares to a Bayes calculation that assumes particular priors.
agent_relevance: Do not copy human jurors' under-weighting. The agent should compute the posterior from stated likelihood ratios and let the number, not a felt sense, set the confidence.

source: Juror comprehension of forensic expert testimony: a literature review and gap analysis (2019)
finding: The weak evidence effect: evidence that only weakly supports one side is sometimes read as supporting the other side. It was strongest for verbal low-strength likelihood ratios. A numeric low-strength LR produced more belief change than the verbal one.
numbers: Reported from Martire et al. (verbal vs numeric LR). Weak evidence effect coined by Fernbach et al. (named in the review).
limits: Secondary report. The weak evidence effect is explained by expectation (jurors expected stronger evidence), not by a proven mechanism.
agent_relevance: When evidence is weak, the agent must still count it for the side it supports. Add a check: does the update have the same sign as the likelihood ratio?

source: Juror comprehension of forensic expert testimony: a literature review and gap analysis (2019)
finding: Laypeople and attorneys often read the random match probability as the chance the defendant is innocent. Some people read an RMP in the opposite direction from the one intended (Thompson et al., as reported).
numbers: No numeric rates given in the review. It adds that the chance of an incorrect association from examiner or system error is generally orders of magnitude higher than the RMP.
limits: Details of the original studies (Thompson and Schumann 1987, Thompson et al.) not opened here, so rates of fallacy use by sample are unknown to this file.
agent_relevance: The agent should not equate a match probability with source probability; add the error-rate term and the prior before reporting a posterior.

source: Juror comprehension of forensic expert testimony: a literature review and gap analysis (2019)
finding: Prior beliefs about the evidence type shape how a number is used. DNA statistics gave belief changes close to intended values; shoeprint statistics were undervalued. Admitting error possibility cut the weight of fingerprint evidence, and a method explanation partly offset that.
numbers: Thompson & Newman (as reported): evidence type (DNA vs shoeprint) mattered more than presentation type (RMP vs LR vs verbal). Koehler et al. (as reported): perceived expert experience was most influential in both an online and an in-person mock trial; method validation modestly raised perceived strength online, none in person.
limits: All secondary. Mock-jury samples.
agent_relevance: Source-credibility cues (reputation, experience) sway human readers more than validity. The agent should score evidence by validity and error rates first, credentials last.

source: Martire, Kemp, Watkins, Sayle, Newell (2013) The expression and interpretation of uncertain forensic science evidence: verbal equivalence, evidence strength, and the weak evidence effect
finding: Two experiments on a larceny trial. Verbal and numeric likelihood ratios gave similar belief change, but both far below Bayesian calculation. Weak inculpatory evidence was 'inverted' to reduce belief in guilt, mostly with verbal wording.
numbers: Exp 1 N=494 (strength low/moderate/high x verbal/numeric). Exp 2 N=411 (inculpatory vs exculpatory, low vs high strength). The weak evidence effect appeared only for inculpatory evidence, mostly verbal.
limits: Abstract read through the Europe PMC record, not the full paper. Undergraduate and MTurk samples. Supports an expectancy account.
agent_relevance: Prefer numbers to verbal labels in the agent's own intermediate scores, and check that a weak LR is not flipped in sign.

source: Mock juror evaluations of forensic conclusion formats within a complete expert report (2025)
finding: A null result: inside a full shoeprint report, the conclusion format (likelihood ratio, random match probability, verbal label, categorical) did not change evidence weight or verdicts. This challenges the worry that statistics confuse lay readers more than categorical claims.
limits: MTurk, 30-40 min study. Null result, so low power for small effects. Report quality and individual differences (comprehension, numeracy, scientific reasoning) predicted weight (adj R2 .257 Exp 1, .343 Exp 2).
agent_relevance: Format effects shown in short-snippet studies may shrink in context. The robust lever is the reader's skill and the report's content, which matches an agent that reads the whole report and reasons about it.

source: Mock juror evaluations of forensic conclusion formats within a complete expert report (2025)
finding: Individual differences matter more than format: comprehension, numeracy, scientific reasoning and need for cognition together explain a substantial share of how much weight the evidence gets.
numbers: Regression of evidence weight on CASOC comprehension, SRS, subjective and objective numeracy, NFC and FEEBS bias subscales: F(7,438)=22.99, adj R2=.257 (Exp 1); F(7,305)=24.32, adj R2=.343 (Exp 2). Condition was ignored in these models.
limits: Exploratory analysis, Bonferroni-corrected predictors, MTurk.
agent_relevance: Skill, not display, is the lever. Supports giving the agent explicit procedures (a trained skill) instead of better wording alone.

source: de Roo, Stevens, de Poot (2026) The impact of institutional authority on forensic evidence evaluation by criminal justice professionals
finding: Dutch judges, prosecutors and defence lawyers could not tell a sound forensic report from an unsound one. The prosecutor's fallacy was noticed only seven times.
numbers: N=133 professionals each rated a sound and an unsound report. Reliability: sound M=3.3 vs unsound M=3.1, F(1)=2.839, p=.094. Only 32% rated the unsound report unreliable; 50% rated the sound one reliable. Evidential strength sound 2.8 vs unsound 2.9, p=.647. Prosecutor's fallacy mentioned 7 times (6 in the pathology report, 1 in the bloodstain report). Pathology rated more reliable than bloodstain pattern analysis (M 3.3 vs 3.0, p=.004).
limits: Online questionnaire, reports built for the study, self-selected volunteers. Reports from well-known institutions got less critical reading, which the authors tie to institutional authority.
agent_relevance: Experts spot the fallacy rarely when it is hidden in a report. The agent needs an active checklist (direction of conditional, base rate, alternative hypotheses), because passive noticing fails even in trained humans.

source: Hefter, Hinkel, Hinkel (2026) Clinical expertise and cognitive reflection predict fewer misconceptions in Bayesian diagnostic reasoning
finding: Medical students and doctors mostly fail Bayesian diagnostic tasks, and wrong answers carry high confidence. Only senior specialists scored near zero on a confidence-weighted score.
numbers: N=86 (56 students, 30 physicians). Incorrect answers ranged from 65.1% (colorectal item) to 93.0% (corona item). 74.4% had negative confidence-weighted scores on the hardest item. All groups except specialists had negative scores on every item. Mean CRT about 0.6.
limits: Online survey, small N, medical (not legal) context. The score is new and unvalidated outside this paper.
agent_relevance: Confident-wrong is the dangerous state. Pair every posterior with a stated confidence and an explicit check against a counts table.

source: Feufel, Keller, Kendel, Spies (2023) Boosting for insight and/or agency: how to maximise accurate test interpretation with natural frequencies
finding: Two levers add up: natural frequencies (insight) and short training on translating to frequencies and applying Bayes (agency). Best results needed both.
numbers: N=577 medical students, pre/post design, registered trial. Conditional probabilities 34% correct; natural frequencies without training 68%; training then probabilities 64%; training plus natural frequencies 89%.
limits: Abstract only was read. Medical students, immediate post-test, no long delay.
agent_relevance: Combine a fixed reformulation step in the scaffold (the agent's own natural-frequency rewrite) with the habit of using it; the effect sizes are large and stack.

source: Kim et al. (2024) Natural frequency tree- vs conditional probability formula-based training for medical students
finding: A randomised trial found that a tree-and-frequency training was no better than formula training overall, but it was better for students with no earlier formula training.
numbers: N=231 medical students, 15-minute videos. Post-test 87.13% (tree) vs 86.03% (formula), p=.86. One month 72.39% vs 68.10%, p=.40. Transfer 75.54% vs 71.43%, p=.41. For students without prior training: follow-up 74.86% vs 58.71% (p=.02); transfer 82.86% vs 66.13% (p=.04).
limits: Abstract only was read. Korean medical schools. Gains faded over one month in both arms. A failed or conditional replication of the strong frequency advantage.
agent_relevance: Frequency format is not a free win once the reasoner has a competing method. Test which route the agent actually uses and measure it on its own problems.

source: Repeated exposure rivals lightweight training in Bayesian inference (2026)
finding: Mere repeated practice on natural-frequency problems raised accuracy a lot, and highlighted-text or animated-visual training added no consistent benefit. Gains held 8 to 10 days and carried to the unpracticed predictive value.
numbers: N=256 laypeople, three arms (exposure only, text training, dynamic training), pre-test, immediate post-test, delayed post-test, generalisation. PPV: no training 34.9% to 59.9% to 58.5%; textual 38.6% to 65.7% to 64.3%; dynamic 48.8% to 70.8% to 65.5%. Phase effect chi2(3)=329.11, p<.001; immediate post vs pre OR=53.70; training main effect chi2(2)=0.57, p=.753.
limits: Online lay sample, natural-frequency format throughout, only an 8-10 day delay.
agent_relevance: Repetition with feedback on similar problems is the active ingredient. For an agent: keep a library of worked Bayes cases and retrieve the nearest one.

source: Fenwick, Campitelli, Thompson (2026) Explaining success in Bayesian reasoning with the adaptive toolbox and expertise
finding: A new account says Bayesian competence is a set of learned tools, not one privileged format. Accuracy rises with training, visualisation, numeracy and domain knowledge, and can be high in mathematically trained people even with probabilities.
numbers: Theory paper; no new data in the part read.
limits: Only the abstract was read. It argues against a single ecological-rationality or nested-sets explanation; it does not give a decisive experiment.
agent_relevance: Rival accounts both predict that making set relations explicit helps. A sound scaffold implements both: counts and a nested set diagram.

source: Qiu, Sha, Allen, Kim, Linzen, van Steenkiste (2025) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in large language models
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs (Gemma 2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5, 7B to 70B) update beliefs poorly over five rounds of a flight-preference task and often stop improving after the first round. Chain-of-thought prompting, numeric formats and 30 rounds did not fix it.
numbers: 624 simulated users, 5 rounds, accuracy on 100 new option sets after each round. Humans (48 users) improved from round 1 to 5 (p=0.002) and sat between small and large LLMs, all below the exact Bayesian assistant. After fine-tuning on the Bayesian assistant's guesses, tuned models agreed with it about 80% of the time and generalised to hotels and a web-shopping task.
limits: Preference inference, not legal evidence. Small open models. Fine-tuning is training, which our scaffold cannot do.
agent_relevance: Prompting tricks alone failed on sequential Bayesian updating. A scaffold that computes the update outside the model (tool or code) is the safer route.

source: Nafar, Venable, Kordjamshidi (2024) Reasoning over uncertain text by generative LLMs (BLInD)
finding: On text descriptions of Bayesian networks, plain prompting collapses as networks grow. Moving the computation to code or a probabilistic logic engine fixes most of it.
numbers: BLInD, networks with 2 to 10 variables. GPT-4 chain-of-thought zero-shot: 79% (V2), 63% (V3), 27% (V4), then 6 to 17 on larger nets; basic QA few-shot near 0 to 3%. PAL (write Python) for GPT-4 fell from 99% (V2) to 10% (V10); Monte Carlo 100% to 88%; ProbLog 99% to 96% (V10). Llama3 Monte Carlo on V10 64%.
limits: Synthetic networks, quantities given as explicit percentages, not courtroom text. Results vary by model.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence for tool use: have the LLM translate a case into a formal network and run exact or sampled inference rather than doing arithmetic in prose.

source: Wang & Redelmeier (2025) Forewarning artificial intelligence about cognitive biases
finding: Telling GPT-4 to 'keep in mind cognitive biases and other pitfalls of reasoning' barely reduced bias, made answers longer, and mostly named the wrong bias. GPT-4 showed no base-rate neglect in this task with or without the warning.
numbers: 10 clinical vignettes, 100 synthetic physicians per version. Forewarned answers 213 vs 138 words; discussed a bias 44.3% vs 0.4% of the time; correct bias named in only 5%; average bias reduction 6.9%. Framing 66% to 45% (p=.003); aggregate-individual 52% to 27%; Occam's razor rose 77% to 89% (p=.024).
quote: synthetic physicians were immune to base-rate neglect and capitulating-to-pressure regardless of forewarning
limits: One model (gpt-4-0613), clinical not legal vignettes. Base-rate neglect item was easy for GPT-4.
agent_relevance: A generic 'be careful' instruction is nearly useless; use task-specific checks instead.

source: Evaluating the o1 reasoning LLM for cognitive bias: a vignette study (2025)
finding: A reasoning model (o1) showed no base-rate neglect and little bias in 7 of 10 clinical scenarios. It did show hindsight bias, a post-hoc fallacy, and a full Occam's-razor reversal.
numbers: 1,800 responses (90 per version per scenario). Base-rate neglect: 100% correct in both high and low prevalence. Hindsight: 100% vs 47.8% (diff 52.2, p<.001). Post hoc fallacy: 18.9% vs 1.1% (diff 17.8). Occam's razor: 100% vs 0% (diff 100, p<.001). Consistency above 94% in 8 of 10 scenarios.
limits: Comparison figures for GPT-4 and clinicians are taken from earlier papers, not a same-run comparison. Only a single easy prevalence item.
agent_relevance: Simple base-rate use is largely solved in current reasoning models; the failures are in structure (competing causes, hindsight, one-sided story). Spend scaffold effort there.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) Thinking fast and slow in large language models
finding: Older LLMs (GPT-3) answer intuitively and wrongly like people on reflection tests, but ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 avoid most traps. Chain-of-thought and examples raised correct answers sharply.
numbers: Cognitive Reflection Test items: correct 59% for ChatGPT-3.5 and 96% for ChatGPT-4; intuitive answers 15% (3.5) and 0% (4) versus 80% for davinci-003. For davinci-003, chain-of-thought lifted correct from 5% to 28%. With 10 or more examples correct went from 18% to over 64% in one study.
limits: CRT and semantic illusions, not Bayes or legal items. Models are older than current ones.
agent_relevance: Warns that results depend on model generation; old benchmark findings on bias should be re-tested on the model we actually use.

source: An LLM canary in the online data coalmine: Bayesian reasoning problems as a capability-gap test (2026)
finding: Online participants using LLMs answered Bayes problems far above human ceilings, so these problems detect LLM use. This implies that current LLMs solve standard textbook Bayes problems well.
numbers: Two preregistered pilots, N=148. In Pilot 2, 57% of participants scored a perfect 5 of 5, against a meta-analytic human ceiling near 24% for a single natural-frequency problem.
limits: Abstract only. Inferred LLM use, not measured model accuracy directly.
agent_relevance: Standard-format Bayes problems are a poor test for a modern LLM; our tests should use messy case text where the hypothesis, base rate and likelihoods must be extracted.

source: Fenton, Neil, Berger (2016) Bayes and the Law
finding: Anchor source for this subfield: argues that the prosecutor's fallacy is the commonest misuse of probability in court and that Bayesian networks can model whole cases. Full text could not be retrieved this session (Europe PMC returned a server error; the PMC page was behind a browser check).
numbers: Not read, no figures recorded.
limits: Not opened. Treat as a pointer only until read. The claim in this line is from memory of the paper's thesis, not from this session.
agent_relevance: Another pass should read it for case-level BN examples.

source: Algorithms on trial: does evaluative probabilistic reporting of forensic evidence infringe the presumption of innocence? (2025)
finding: Critics say likelihood ratios usurp the jury's function and conflict with the presumption of innocence. The paper argues this rests on a misunderstanding of what the expert is asked to do and of the presumption itself.
numbers: Qualitative legal argument. Quoted criticism: LRs 'have no place in criminal trials'.
limits: Opened the abstract and introduction only. One author's position; contested.
agent_relevance: A boundary condition: the agent should report evidence strength as a likelihood ratio, and keep prior odds and the final verdict with the human decision maker.

source: First impressions matter: mundane obstacles to a forensic device for probabilistic reporting in fingerprint analysis (2025)
finding: Statistics have changed little in fingerprint practice, and the cause is mostly practical: no accessible software, data sets, market or training, rather than only resistance or legal apathy.
numbers: Interview study, no effect sizes.
limits: Opened abstract and introduction only. Small interview sample.
agent_relevance: Adoption depends on usable tools. Reinforces the case for giving the agent a callable Bayes routine, not just advice.
